results.title: Neuron type classification
results.question: What types of Kenyon cells exist in the adult Drosophila brain?
results.response: The adult Drosophila brain contains multiple types of Kenyon cells. VFB records show that there are several types, including [[KCab-c](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00110929 "Open KCab-c in Virtual Fly Brain")(i)](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00049111 "Open KCab-c(i) in Virtual Fly Brain"), KCab-c, [KCg-m](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111061 "Open KCg-m in Virtual Fly Brain"), [[Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003686 "Open Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain") of main calyx](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047926 "Open Kenyon cell of main calyx in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [gamma Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100247 "Open gamma Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain"). Additionally, VFB data indicates that Kenyon cells can be classified into three main subtypes: alpha/beta, alpha'/beta', and gamma Kenyon cells, which can be further subdivided into subtypes such as core, surface, posterior, anterior-posterior, middle, dorsal, and main. VFB holds [37](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of Kenyon cell") records of subclasses of Kenyon cell, providing further information on the diversity of Kenyon cell types. To explore the different types of Kenyon cells in more detail, you can access the list of available images of Kenyon cell, scRNAseq data for Kenyon cell, or transgene expression in Kenyon cell through VFB.

results.title: Central complex structure
results.question: What are the main components of the Drosophila central complex and what functions are they associated with?
results.response:
To address the question about the main components of the Drosophila central complex and their associated functions, we must consider the available data and literature. 

The Drosophila central complex is a critical structure in the insect brain, known for its role in regulating various behaviors and cognitive functions. It is composed of several distinct substructures, each with specific roles and connections within the brain.

VFB does not currently hold detailed, specific data on the main components of the Drosophila central complex or their functions. However, it is known from the literature (Wolff et al., 2015; Heinze et al., 2013) that the central complex in Drosophila melanogaster includes components such as the ellipsoid body, the fan-shaped body, the noduli, and the protocerebral bridge. These components are involved in a range of functions including spatial memory, visual navigation, and the control of locomotor activity.

Given the absence of specific data within VFB on this topic, a narrower follow-up would require consulting detailed neuroanatomical studies or databases that specialize in Drosophila brain structures and their functions. results.title: Neuron characterisation
results.question: What is known about the LPLC2 visual neuron type? Where is it, what does it connect to, and what is its function?
results.response: The LPLC2 visual neuron type is described as a lobula plate-lobula columnar neuron. According to the information available from VFB, its cell body lies in the dorsal area of the lateral cell body rind, as noted by Wu et al., 2016. It has a distinct dendritic arbor in each lobula plate layer, extending outwards from the main fiber in the direction of motion detection for the layer, as described by Klapoetke et al., 2017. VFB does not currently hold specific data on the connections of the LPLC2 visual neuron type beyond its dendritic arbor structure. The function of the LPLC2 visual neuron type is related to motion detection, given the direction of its dendritic arbor in each lobula plate layer. For more detailed information on its connectivity and function, further queries can be made to explore available datasets and publications.

According to VFB, the [adult antennal lobe](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00007401 "Open adult antennal lobe in Virtual Fly Brain") is more elaborated than the larval antennal lobe. VFB records show that the organisation of the antennal lobe in adult Drosophila has approximately 50 glomeruli, whereas in larval Drosophila it has around 22 glomeruli. 

VFB holds a range of data related to the antennal lobe, including images, neuron information, parts and subclasses of the antennal lobe, and tracts/nerves innervating it. For example, VFB has annotated [676](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003924,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in antennal lobe") neurons with some part in the antennal lobe, and [17046](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003924,ImagesNeurons "Run in VFB: Images of neurons with some part in antennal lobe") images of neurons with some part in the antennal lobe.

results.title: Bidirectional connectivity
results.question: Are there reciprocal connections between mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) and dopaminergic neurons (DANs)? Which pairs have the strongest mutual connectivity?
results.response:
The connectome data indicates that there are reciprocal connections between mushroom body output neurons and dopaminergic neurons. VFB records show 22 reciprocal class-level pairs between these two neuron types. The direction from [dopaminergic neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005131 "Open dopaminergic neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") to [mushroom body output neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047953 "Open mushroom body output neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") has a partner count of 77, while the direction from mushroom body output neuron to dopaminergic neuron has a partner count of 94. The target-to-source weight is 7620 and the source-to-target weight is 2697, as found by VFB's reciprocal connectivity query. 

VFB has annotated a large number of connectivity records for both mushroom body output neurons and dopaminergic neurons, including [2788](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for MBON") downstream and [2077](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for MBON") upstream connectivity classes for mushroom body output neurons, and [8845](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005131,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for dopaminergic neuron") downstream and [7914](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005131,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for dopaminergic neuron") upstream connectivity classes for dopaminergic neurons. 

To identify the specific pairs with the strongest mutual connectivity, you can explore the top_partners data provided by VFB's reciprocal connectivity query.

results.response:
The connectome data indicates that several neuron types might mediate a connection between the [visual system](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047735 "Open visual system in Virtual Fly Brain") and the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain"). VFB records show that neurons such as [ML-VPN2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052139 "Open ML-VPN2 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mt-VPN1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052141 "Open Mt-VPN1 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mt-VPN](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052140 "Open Mt-VPN in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mti](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052142 "Open Mti in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [T4ai neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052241 "Open T4ai neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") have some part in the visual system. Furthermore, the pathway evidence suggests that adult visual projection neurons, which have presynaptic terminals in the mushroom body, might also mediate this connection, as reported by Vogt et al., 2016.

The connectivity between these neurons could potentially allow visual information to reach the memory circuit, given the presence of neurons with presynaptic and postsynaptic terminals in both the visual system and the mushroom body.
